name: Prophia on AI in Commercial Real Estate: Lease Abstraction and Agentic Adoption
title: Prophia on AI in Commercial Real Estate: Lease Abstraction and Agentic Adoption
answer: Prophia's site is the blog and product literature of a commercial real estate document-AI vendor founded in 2018. Its most useful material explains how lease abstraction works in production: models trained since 2018 on roughly 100,000 private CRE documents, recognising over 200 lease terms, with human review of the final third of annotations. It also reports a May 2026 survey finding 66% of CRE professionals use AI weekly or daily while only 5% trust it for deal decisions.

sections.body: This is the website of Prophia, a commercial real estate technology company founded in 2018 by Cameron Steele and Chris Hsu. The pages read are the company's blog, mixing explanatory articles, case studies, survey reports and news commentary, plus product claims about its lease abstraction platform. The material spans posts on generative and vertical AI, data privacy, agentic AI, digital transformation and AI adoption among smaller firms. Several posts carry 2026 dates, including a May 2026 survey report and a Realcomm 2026 reference. The site is a vendor's own publication, so product claims are self-reported.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The central argument across these pages is that commercial real estate is a vertical AI problem, not a general one. Prophia says its models were built over five years on approximately 100,000 proprietary CRE documents, with training data dating to 2018 and drawn from leading CRE firms in the Northern Hemisphere under explicit customer permission. The system recognises over 200 CRE terms and concepts found in standardised leases, and can brief leases, run reports, abstract data into lease abstracts and generate dynamic stacking plans. On accuracy, the company states it reaches 100% accuracy by combining computer-generated synthesis with human review; CEO Cameron Steele says each onboarded tenant involves about seven documents, roughly two-thirds of annotations are automated, and the remaining third goes through technical audits and human review taking 30 to 40 minutes per tenant. The agentic AI posts argue that autonomous agents monitoring lease expirations, ingesting due diligence folders and handling tenant communications depend on clean, verified, traceable lease data, and identify three failure points: abstraction inconsistency across a portfolio, amendment and version gaps, and original lease data not being the operative document. The privacy post sets out Prophia's practices, including OWASP Top 10 and SOC 2 adherence.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Prophia says its first model iteration used approximately 100,000 proprietary CRE documents, that training began around 2019 and dates to 2018 client relationships, and that its AI recognises over 200 CRE terms. It reports 650M+ square feet represented on its platform and 100% abstraction accuracy through human and machine synthesis. A May 2026 survey by First American Data & Analytics and DealGround, covering 255 CRE professionals, found 66% use AI weekly or daily, over 42% daily, 53% restrict it to support work, 17% use it only with heavy manual verification, and just 5% trust it to inform a deal decision. Other cited figures include proptech investment of $16.7 billion in 2025, up 67.9%, Gartner's projection that a third of enterprise applications will include agentic AI by 2028, and Gartner's expectation that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For anyone following AI in real estate, this source is useful because it describes a document-AI system in production rather than in pilot. The lease abstraction workflow, the split between automated annotation and human review, the training corpus and the recognition of standard lease terms give a concrete picture of how extraction is actually delivered. The survey and agentic AI posts frame the adoption gap that matters to practitioners: high weekly use alongside low trust for deal decisions, and data quality named as the main blocker to autonomous agents. The failure points listed for agentic AI over portfolios are a practical checklist for anyone assessing lease data readiness.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: The pages are published by Prophia and promote its platform, so accuracy, scale and training-data claims are self-reported and not independently verified. Several posts are dated 2026 and rely on third-party surveys and analyst projections that readers would need to check at source. The material is largely qualitative and US or Northern Hemisphere focused, with little detail on pricing, implementation effort or performance outside standardised leases. It does not offer independent benchmarking of lease abstraction tools, and the agentic AI discussion is forward-looking rather than a report of deployed systems.
